final_message:
All five versions build with their own `build.cmd` and give byte-identical output on the sample and on six generated test files.

**Testing.** `samples/` has only `s1`, so I wrote a Python reference that uses the regex from SPEC.md exactly (`tools/ref.py`). It matches `s1.out`. A generator (`tools/gen.py`) made more inputs, checked against that reference:
- `t1`–`t4`: 30 to 200,000 lines with 3 to 3,000 templates, many kinds of malformed line, odd but valid inputs (status `000`, latencies with leading zeros, quotes inside the query string, empty user agent, `//` paths) and ties in the top-10.
- `t5`: lines of about 10,000 characters and a last line without a newline.
- `big`: 2,000,000 lines, 168 MB. I deleted this one afterwards to save disk space.

**Algorithm (the same in all five).** Each program reads the file in 4 MB chunks and only parses whole lines. It never runs a regex. Each line goes through one hand-written parser, front to back. A `\n` fails every rule in the grammar, so the parser always stops at the end of its own line without needing bounds checks, and the newline search is done in the same pass. While it checks the path, the parser builds the template (`{id}` for all-digit segments) in a scratch buffer, so no strings are created per line. Templates are stored in a hash table with each template's latencies in a growable array. At the end it sorts the templates (count descending, then byte order) and takes the top 10. For p50 and p95 it uses quickselect rather than a full sort; the maximum is the largest value at or above the p95 position.

**Choices for speed in each version:**
- **C++:** raw pointers; an SSE2 search for the closing `"` or newline; `memchr` only to skip malformed lines; a hand-written hash table; `std::nth_element`; unbuffered `fread`; stdout set to binary mode so it prints `\n`, not `\r\n`.
- **Go:** slice indexing laid out so the compiler can drop most bounds checks; `bytes.IndexByte`; a `map[string]*template` looked up with `m[string(b)]`, which doesn't allocate.
- **Java:** a parser over `byte[]` that returns the next line's position, kept as a small method so the JIT compiles it fully; an FNV-hashed table on byte keys; `long[]` latency arrays.
- **C#:** `unsafe` pointer parsing; vectorised `IndexOfAny('"', '\n')` and `LastIndexOf`; pinned scratch buffers; a hand-written hash table.
- **JS:** a byte loop over a `Buffer`; template keys in typed arrays with an FNV hash and open addressing, so no strings per line; `Float64Array` latency arrays; `Buffer.indexOf` only to skip malformed lines.

**Rough timings** on the 168 MB file (the machine was busy, so these are noisy best-of-several runs): C++ about 330 ms, Go about 350 ms, C# about 550 ms, Java about 1.05 s and Node about 1.07 s. I didn't get a usable peak-memory figure.

**Results:** C++, Java, C#, Go and JS each pass `s1` and `t1`–`t5`, and passed `big` before I deleted it.

**Limit:** latencies are held in 64-bit integers, or in doubles for JS. A latency longer than about 18 digits (about 15 in JS) would come out wrong, though it still matches the regex.

My test tools are in `tools/` and the test files in `tests/`, both inside the project folder. To check a version, run `tools/check.sh "<command>"` from Git Bash.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
